core.text: To place one past action before another, Latin uses **the pluperfect (the 'had done' tense)**: *puer ūmidus erat* — the boy was wet — *quod per imbrem ambulāverat*, because he had walked through the rain. Active: perfect stem + -era- + the ordinary endings: *ambulāveram, -erās, -erat, -erāmus, -erātis, -erant*. Passive and deponent: participle + *eram, erās, erat …*: *captus erat* — he had been caught; *profectī erant* — they had set out. Latin name: *plūsquamperfectum indicātīvī*.
English marks it with *had*: *he had come*, *they had gone*. It is the 'past of the past'.
Active: perfect stem + -eram (that is, the perfect infinitive minus -isse, plus -eram). Passive: participle + eram.

invented.la: Puer, quī diū dormīverat, tandem surrēxit.
invented.en: The boy, who had slept a long time, at last got up.

core.text: *Scrīpsit* is **the perfect (the 'did / has done' tense)**: he wrote. *Scrīpserat* adds -era-: he had written, before something else in the story. Find the -era- (or the -erat / -erant with a participle) and you have the pluperfect.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 24) sort out the English: the present perfect (*he has come*) is a sense of the Latin perfect; the past perfect (*he had come*) is the pluperfect. Their examples: *ille vēnerat*, *istī profectī erant*, *vīderāmus*, *advēneram*.

*Sum* has *fueram, fuerās, fuerat …*. In stories the pluperfect often sits in a *postquam*, *quod* or relative clause (*quae rēx fēcerat* — which the king had done) or in a report of the past: *dīxit sē scrīpsisse* becomes *dīxerat …* when the whole scene is earlier.

teach.title: The past before the past
teach.say: One past action can be set earlier than another, and the tense that does it is **the pluperfect (the 'had done' tense)**. *Quīntus dormīverat, sed nunc vigilat* — he had slept; now he is awake. English marks it with 'had': had come, had gone, had written. It never stands for the plain past by itself.

teach.title: Building the active: the perfect stem plus -erat
teach.say: Take the perfect and cut off its ending — *ambulāvī → ambulāv-*, *scrīpsī → scrīps-*, *clausī → claus-* — then add *-erat* for 'he or she had': *ambulāverat*, *scrīpserat*, *clauserat*. It is the very *erat* you already know, glued on the end.

show.say: ambulāverat — the perfect stem ambulāv- with -erat behind it

teach.title: The other five persons
teach.say: The rest of the row is the ordinary set of endings on the same *-erā-*: *-eram* (I), *-erās* (you), *-erat* (he), *-erāmus* (we), *-erātis* (you all), *-erant* (they). *Ego eum anteā nōn vīderam*; *Vōs ex oppidō iam discesserātis*.

show.say: ambulāveram / ambulāverātis — the same -erā- under every person

teach.title: Passive and deponent take two words
teach.say: A passive, and a deponent (looks passive, means active), build the pluperfect from the participle plus *erat*: *Iānua ā servō clausa erat* — the door had been shut; *Mēdus profectus erat* — Medus had set out. Swap *erat* back for *est* and you are in the perfect again.

teach.title: Telling it from the perfect
teach.say: *Abiit* — he went away; *abierat* — he had gone away, before the rest of the story. In *Iūlius vēnit; Mēdus autem iam abierat* the two tenses do different work in one sentence: *vēnit* moves the story on, *abierat* looks back behind it. Find the *-era-*, or the *erat* beside a participle.
